evals.prompt: I run partnerships at Corvane, we're a data-integration platform with about 40 SI partners. We're relaunching the partner program in Q2 and the new Gold tier will require two Corvane-certified engineers per partner. I need you to design the certification: I'm thinking Associate, Professional and Expert levels, a 60-question proctored exam, two-year validity. Candidates are partner engineers, maybe 120 a year. To be honest our end customers have never asked us whether a partner is certified, they pick partners on price and references, but the partner managers want a credential so Gold means something. Program owner would be me, 4 hours a week, and a solutions architect could take over. Where do we start?
evals.expected_output: A credential-gate verdict stating that Corvane's own Gold-tier requirement is not outside demand and that, with no end customer choosing partners by it, the gate fails as a credential decision. The run recommends a partner implementation review or validator instead, names the observable event that would reopen the credential question, and stops without designing the three-level exam.
expectations: States the gate verdict before any tier, format, proctoring or level design.
States that Corvane's own Gold-tier requirement is not outside demand, because partners comply with it whatever the credential is worth.
Fails the gate as a credential decision, citing that no end customer chooses partners by the credential.
Recommends a partner implementation review or validator of partners' delivered work as the alternative, rather than a test of partner engineers.
Does not deliver the requested Associate, Professional and Expert three-level design.
Does not deliver a 60-question multiple-choice exam design or any exam items.
Names the observable event that would reopen the credential decision: end customers choosing partners by the credential, or a buyer contract or procurement checklist counting certified people.
States that even with end-customer evidence the ceiling would be a skill badge, with role certification only once contracts or tenders count certified people.
Does not adopt the two-year validity or the 60-question format as an industry standard.
Ends the design at the failed gate rather than continuing to interview on dates, budget or blueprint.
States the verdict and its ceiling in one sentence carrying the evidence (no end-customer ask) rather than hedging across paragraphs.

evals.prompt: Lumenshift is a low-code workflow platform. Around 400 freelance consultants and maybe 30 small IT services firms build on it for clients, and clients find them through our 'Find a partner' directory and word of mouth. Several consultants have told us clients ask 'are you certified?' and they have nothing to show. Nobody has put it in a tender yet. Our CEO wants to launch 'Lumenshift Certified Professional' and 'Lumenshift Certified Expert' together in six months, both exam-based, and she wants Expert to be the headline because our best consultants are the ones clients fight over. We ship a major version every year, supported for two years. I'm the education lead with 10 hours a week, a named successor, and budget approved for two years. What's the design?
evals.expected_output: A gate verdict placing the ceiling at skill badge (clients shortlist consultants by it; role certification waits for tenders or contracts counting certified people), 'Professional' delivered as a skill badge with its tier named, the Expert exam refused at launch and replaced by a human-reviewed client project with live defence, one level at launch, an opt-in expert directory, a fee one engagement repays with a free practice quiz, a marketplace-hosted prep course, and 2-3 candidate designs ranked by efficiency with a recommendation awaiting the user's pick.
expectations: States the gate verdict: clients shortlisting freelancers and services firms by the credential, with a ceiling of skill badge.
States that role certification becomes available only once tenders or client contracts count certified people, and names that as the certification trigger.
Labels 'Lumenshift Certified Professional' explicitly as carrying the skill-badge tier rather than treating the level name as a tier of its own.
Refuses to launch the Expert level as an exam, giving the reason that an expert level has the smallest candidate pool, the hardest cut score to defend and the most public failure.
Proposes awarding the Expert level by human-reviewed client project with a short live defence, requiring evidence the client allows the consultant to show, anonymised where needed.
Launches one level and conditions a second on the first being live through one major product version or 12 months, plus a named consumer asking for the distinction.
Recommends the auto-graded hands-on task format for the badge with a human-attributable step, such as a sampled live or recorded explanation announced in the candidate agreement.
Proposes an opt-in 'find a certified expert' directory listing name, firm, credential, region, languages and contact, and names it as the main return on the exam fee for freelancers.
Keys the price to the consumer: a fee one engagement repays, with seat bundles for services firms, plus a published prep path and a free practice quiz.
Recommends hosting the prep course on a public course marketplace because the gate's consumer is freelancers' clients and learners discover the course there.
Binds the badge to the yearly major version with no expiry and a delta path on the next major, rather than re-stamping per release.
Presents 2-3 candidate designs ordered by efficiency with one recommended, and waits for the user's pick rather than delivering a single final design.
Names the outcome metric as something clients do, such as engagements won citing the credential or directory contact requests from clients, not holder counts.
Prefers recommended experience over a hard prerequisite between levels, stating a hard prerequisite adds a second exam fee and sitting for every candidate.

evals.prompt: Can you sanity-check our exam design before we sign the proctoring contract? Brightmoor is an observability platform and the credential is 'Brightmoor Certified Engineer'. Enterprise customers have started writing 'engineers certified on the monitoring platform' into their support contracts, so this is real demand. Design: 60 multiple-choice questions, online, unproctored, 90 minutes, 70% to pass, AI tools strictly prohibited, two parallel forms rotated monthly, item bank of 180 questions written by our support team. We're adding a proctoring vendor that does ID-photo face matching and AI gaze flagging. Candidates sit in Germany, France, Chicago and Bangalore. Validity three years. We have a named owner, a successor and funding for two years. What's wrong with it?
evals.expected_output: A review that deletes unproctored multiple-choice as an assessed credential, declares the AI ban unenforceable, replaces the 70% cut score with a standard-setting method and equating, identifies face matching and gaze flagging as automated face processing with its privacy obligations (BIPA, GDPR DPIA, EU AI Act), separates the proctoring and identity decisions, and places the ceiling at role certification with its full obligation list and a hands-on format.
expectations: Rejects unproctored multiple-choice as an assessed credential, stating it measures search and assistant use, and keeps it only as a free practice quiz.
States the AI ban is unenforceable without live or test-centre proctoring with screen capture, applying the rule never to ban what cannot be detected.
Offers the alternative AI policy of 'allowed', worded so the credential certifies the person working with their own tools.
Rejects the 70% cut score as undefended and names a standard-setting method (modified Angoff, Bookmark or contrasting groups) run by an expert panel.
States that a program that cannot fund one standard-setting panel session should issue a completion badge rather than a pass/fail credential.
Requires equating between the rotated forms via anchor items or a calibrated scale, and states that a scaled score without equating is a relabelled percentage.
Identifies ID-photo face matching and AI gaze flagging as automated face processing, and states that compliance cost follows that processing rather than the proctoring mode.
Requires a privacy review before any automated face processing, a non-biometric path for candidates, and human review of every automated flag before any sanction.
Names Illinois BIPA for the Chicago candidates: a written or electronic release before collecting face geometry and a published retention and destruction schedule.
Names GDPR special-category treatment and a data-protection impact assessment for the German and French candidates, with the proctoring vendor as processor and the duty staying with Brightmoor.
Flags the EU AI Act high-risk listing for AI systems monitoring behaviour during tests and requires checking applicability before deploying AI flagging to EU candidates.
Notes that a human proctor watching a webcam with no face matching sits in the lower compliance-cost group.
Treats 'who watches the sitting' and 'how identity is verified' as two separate decisions.

Places the ceiling at role certification given buyer contracts naming certified engineers, and lists its obligations: job task analysis, standard-setting study, equated forms, item security, real identity check, appeals path, funded renewal cycle.

Recommends hands-on tasks over recall items as the leak and AI countermeasure, promoting the proctored performance exam for this buyer-counted role credential when per-sitting environments are funded.

evals.prompt: Keldrick Data runs a streaming database. Our 'Keldrick Certified Operator' is a real role certification: two enterprise contracts now require named certified operators on the account, we have a named owner and two years of funding. Engineering ships every two weeks and a new major every 12 months, each major supported for 24 months. Current plan for renewal: re-certify every release so the credential is always current, and when v4 lands next spring we void the v3 holders so nobody is certified on an old version. I also looked at what the big cloud vendors do, the industry standard seems to be two or three years with a full-price retake at around $300, so we'd copy that. Sketch the renewal, retake and retirement section for me.
evals.expected_output: A renewal section binding the credential to the supported major version with a weekly re-alignment window derived from Keldrick's cadence, renewal as a hands-on delta task per major with a sampled live explanation, v3 holders kept valid until their own expiry with the version stamped and a path to v4, every vendor figure quoted as that vendor's choice with a read date rather than an industry standard, the fee derived from own costs, a retake rule, and a program retirement rule.
expectations: Binds the credential to the supported major version rather than re-certifying on every biweekly release.
States that biweekly releases re-align the exam continuously and that the credential version changes only when the blueprint changes.
Sets a written re-alignment window in weeks per release derived from Keldrick's own cadence, with checkers or item review run against each release.
Recommends renewal as a short hands-on delta task on each new major version covering only what changed, with the same sampled live explanation as the initial award.
States the reason the delta task carries a sampled live explanation: renewal must not become the proxy-sitting route.
Refuses to void v3 holders when v4 lands; keeps them valid until their own expiry while v3 is supported, stamps the version passed, and offers a path to the replacement.
Requires the v3 exam retirement to be announced in advance.
Rejects the 'industry standard' framing, quotes any vendor validity or retake figure as that vendor's own choice with its read date, and labels every number in the section as sourced or self-set.
Does not copy a $300 fee or a two-to-three-year validity from other vendors; derives any fee from Keldrick's own break-even per attempt.
States that full-price and discounted retakes carry an equal currency signal because both re-test the full blueprint, and that price changes who renews, not what renewal proves.
Notes that activity-based renewal proves exposure to changes, not competence on them.
Writes a retake rule with a waiting period after a fail, an attempt cap per window, and whether the fee recurs.
Adds a program retirement rule: honour every unexpired credential, keep verification live for a stated period, refund or honour sold vouchers.

evals.prompt: Numbers time for the Tessara Payments integrator badge. Context: freelance integrators pass a hands-on badge to get listed in our integrator directory, which merchants already browse to pick someone. Costs I have: 38,000 to build the first version (authoring, environments, pilot, standard setting, issuing setup), we expect that version to live two years, about 9,000 a year to keep it aligned and run appeals, and 22 per sitting for hosting and payment fees. We expect 500 attempts a year and about 350 passes. My plan: the closest competitor charges 150 so we charge 149, and we hand out 2,000 free voucher codes at meetups this year to hit our goal of 1,000 certified integrators by December, which is the number the board signed off on. Build the pricing and the success section.
evals.expected_output: A pricing section that computes the break-even fee per attempt from Tessara's own figures (about 78), rejects the competitor-anchored 149 and the cost-per-holder trap, keys the fee to freelancers with seat bundles and a free practice quiz, writes voucher rules and models them as their own line, and a success section whose outcome metric is merchant behaviour, with holder count demoted to a health signal, a live verified holder count offered in place of the board's target, and a dated kill rule.
expectations: Computes the break-even fee per attempt from Tessara's own costs: yearly fixed 38,000 / 2 = 19,000, plus yearly operating 9,000, divided by 500 attempts, plus 22 per sitting, arriving at about 78 per attempt.
Rejects pricing at 149 because it is derived from a competitor's price rather than own costs.
Does not set the fee equal to cost per certified holder, and states that doing so recovers failed attempts twice.
Charges the fee per attempt so failed attempts pay their own sitting cost.
Keys the fee to freelancers selling to clients: a fee one engagement repays, with seat bundles for firms.
Requires a published prep path and a free practice quiz because freelancers pay from their own pocket and lose billable days studying.
Specifies voucher rules: expiry date, single use, no resale, tracked by campaign.
Models vouchers as their own line that lowers revenue per attempt without lowering cost, and flags that 2,000 vouchers against 500 expected attempts breaks the break-even arithmetic.
States that voucher-driven sittings must never be reported as organic demand.
Rejects 1,000 certified integrators as the success metric and classifies holder count as a health signal only.
Names the outcome metric as something merchants do, such as directory contact requests from merchants or engagements won citing the badge.
Offers a live, verified holder count on the verification page as the substitute for the board's holder target.
Sets a kill rule before launch as a number and a calendar date, labelled as a self-set baseline.

evals.prompt: Orvalon is an IoT device-management platform. Our 'Orvalon Certified Integrator' badge has run for a year with about 200 holders, and three training companies in Poland, Brazil and India want to deliver it. Proposed deal: they teach the official prep course, run the exam sittings on their own premises for their students, and we pay them 40% of the exam fee for every student who passes. To make the course excellent, our lead item writer Tomasz will write the official prep course, and since our MOOC platform already has a quiz engine we'll move the actual exam into the course so students finish and get certified in one place. The training companies also asked for the current item bank so their course matches the exam. Write up the partner model.
evals.expected_output: A partner model that refuses the item-bank share, keeps training partners from proctoring their own students, converts the per-pass revenue share into a share on vouchers sold, removes the item writer from prep-course authoring, keeps the assessed exam off the MOOC quiz engine, keeps the award decision with Orvalon, and sets authorisation criteria, yearly audits, a published partner list, revocation grounds, and separate processor contracts for exam delivery.
expectations: Refuses to share the live item bank with training partners.
Refuses to let training partners proctor or run sittings for their own students, separating teaching from exam delivery.
Rejects the 40%-per-pass revenue share as a share of passes, and allows a revenue share on exam vouchers sold through trainers instead.
Removes Tomasz, the item writer, from prep-course authoring, stating that item writers never author prep courses.
Keeps the assessed exam off the MOOC platform because its built-in quizzes are unproctored and only the vendor awards the credential.
Keeps the award decision with Orvalon even when a delivery partner runs the sitting.
Sets authorisation criteria for each trainer: holds the credential, passes a teach-back session, uses the official blueprint.
Commits to auditing a sample of training sessions yearly and publishing the authorised partner list.
Names pass guarantees and leaked items as grounds for revoking a training partner's authorisation.
Lists what prep material may carry: the blueprint, domain weights, retired sample items and practice environments.
Contracts exam-delivery partners (test-centre networks or online proctoring services) as processors, with Orvalon keeping the item bank, the cut score and the award decision.
States the economics split: training partners earn from course fees, the vendor earns from exam fees or partner-tier fees.

evals.prompt: Pellmont makes a CI/CD platform. Our user conference is in nine weeks and the CEO announced on stage last year that 'Pellmont Certified Associate' would be available at this one, so it has to exist. Hiring managers at two customers have told us they'd screen for it. I'm the developer advocate building it, but I'm leaving the company in three months and nobody has been named to take it over; budget is a few thousand. I want a proctored exam with a proper cut score, 100 questions, ready for conference day. What's the plan?
evals.expected_output: A plan that deletes every assessed tier because no standing owner exists, ships a completion badge for conference day with its tier named, states which answer moved which option, places the gate ceiling at skill badge with job posts naming it as the trigger, writes the observable event that reopens the assessed tier, sets a dated go/no-go with a named fallback, and refuses the 100-question proctored exam.
expectations: Deletes every tier that asserts competence (skill badge and role certification) because no standing owner with recurring weekly hours and a named successor exists, and says so.
Recommends a completion badge for conference day, stating it claims attendance only, with no cut score and no expiry.
States which interview answer moved which option: the nine-week date promoting the completion badge, the departing owner with no successor deleting the assessed tiers.
Places the gate ceiling at skill badge given hiring-manager demand, and names job posts naming the badge as the trigger for anything higher.
Labels 'Pellmont Certified Associate' with the tier it carries at launch (completion badge) rather than letting the level name imply a certification.
Does not deliver a 100-question proctored exam or a cut score for conference day.
Writes the observable event that reopens the assessed tier: a named owner with weekly hours and a successor, plus funding for standard setting.
Sets a dated go/no-go check weeks before the conference with the fallback named.
Names the auto-graded hands-on task, not multiple-choice, as the format for the later skill badge.
States that a program that cannot fund one standard-setting panel session must issue a completion badge rather than a pass/fail credential.
Tells the hiring managers which tier the credential is rather than presenting the completion badge as a certification.

evals.prompt: Grab bag from our platform team at Veldora this week, can you sort it out: (1) our partner Nimbletide wants their connector marked 'Veldora Certified' in our marketplace, (2) HR wants a skills matrix with levels for our 40 internal engineers, (3) I personally need to pass the Terraform Associate next month, (4) leadership is asking whether we should build a Veldora Academy at all, and (5) someone suggested a badge for the consultants who build on us. Which of these should we actually work on, and how?
evals.expected_output: A scope check that routes the connector certification to the app-marketplace-review skill, declines the internal skills matrix and the Terraform prep as out of scope, routes the Academy question to developer-education-strategy, keeps only the consultant badge, and opens it with the first credential-gate question asked on its own.
expectations: Routes the Nimbletide connector certification to samber/developer-platform-skills@app-marketplace-review, stating it certifies an app rather than a person.
Declines the internal skills matrix as out of scope because no outside reader relies on it, and points it to people or L&D teams.
Declines to help with Terraform Associate preparation, stating that a candidate preparing for someone else's exam is out of scope, and stops on that item.
Routes the Academy question to samber/developer-relations-skills@developer-education-strategy and says to return once a credential is on the table.
Keeps only the consultant badge in scope.
Opens the consultant badge with the credential gate: asks who outside Veldora will act on the credential and what they will do differently.
Asks interview questions one per message rather than listing all of them at once.
Does not design a tier, format or exam for the consultant badge before the gate questions are answered.
Does not produce a Terraform study plan or any exam preparation material.

evals.prompt: Something's off with the Halvane CDN 'Edge Operator' badge. Pass rate on form B went from 58% in Q1 to 91% in Q3; form A stayed around 60%. Most Q3 candidates came from two reseller partners who pay for seats under their partner tier. The exam is auto-graded hands-on tasks in a sandbox, unproctored, with account login. My plan: switch to proctored multiple choice, add a strict no-AI rule, and reset the badge of everyone who passed form B in Q3. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: A leak response that reads the form-B jump as a leak or unattended-agent signal, runs the incident runbook in order, contains by pulling form B, investigates before sanctioning, replaces the blanket reset with per-agreement revocation and appeal, names proxy sitting because partners pay, keeps the hands-on format with a sampled human-attributable step, rejects multiple-choice and the undetectable AI ban, and adds item exposure monitoring.
expectations: Reads the form-B pass-rate jump against a flat form A as the first leak signal, or as tasks now solvable unattended by agents, rather than as improved candidates.
Follows the incident runbook in order: detect, contain, investigate, decide, recover, record.
Contains by pulling form B and switching to reserve forms before investigating.
Investigates with item exposure data and candidate statements before any sanction.
Rejects the blanket reset of every Q3 form-B pass; revokes only per the candidate agreement, with an appeals path.
Names proxy sitting as the threat because the reseller partners pay for seats, and counters it with spot live verification or a short defence on a sample of passes.
Rejects switching to proctored multiple-choice, stating that recall items are what assistants answer best and what leaks worst.
Rejects the strict no-AI rule for an unproctored sitting because it cannot be detected, and offers the 'allowed' policy with a human-attributable step instead.
Keeps the hands-on format and adds a sampled live or recorded explanation announced in the candidate agreement.
Recovers by writing replacement task variants, re-equating, and filing takedown requests if a dump site is found.
Adds item exposure analysis as a standing control: retire tasks whose success rate jumps, and monitor pass rate per item and per form.
Records what changed so the next leak is caught sooner.

evals.prompt: Sindral's feature-flag platform, 'Sindral Certified Engineer' skill badge, aimed at the agency developers our customers hire; agencies already ask us for a way to prove their people know the product. Here's my draft so you can turn it into a build plan: blueprint is our eight product features, each weighted 12.5%; three task variants per feature; cut score 75% of checks passed; we skip the pilot because we only have eleven friendly agency devs and that's not enough data anyway; I have 120 hours total across the next four months and no reviewers; accommodation requests go in the candidate's record so support can see the history. Also, candidates are in Quebec and Ontario, fine to call them Certified Engineers?
evals.expected_output: A build plan that rebuilds the blueprint from a job task analysis weighted by frequency and cost of error, keeps the pilot for clarity and checker correctness, sizes against the 120-hour ceiling by cutting variants or domains rather than the pilot or review, adds reviewer hours, replaces the percentage cut score with panel-written end-state checks, moves accommodation documentation out of the candidate record, warns on the regulated 'engineer' title in Canadian provinces, and labels every hour as self-set.
expectations: Rejects the feature-list blueprint and derives domains from a job task analysis: practitioner interviews, escalated support tickets, implementation reviews.
Weights domains by task frequency and the cost of doing the task wrong, not equal 12.5% shares.
Requires publishing the domains and weights so candidates can hold the program to them.
Keeps the pilot despite only eleven candidates, using it for task clarity and checker correctness and deferring item statistics until live volume accrues.
States that no task is scored before it has been piloted.
Sizes the build against the 120-hour ceiling and, where it does not fit, cuts variants or domains, never the pilot or the review.
Adds review hours (technical accuracy by a second expert plus a bias and clarity review) and flags 'no reviewers' as a gap in the plan.
Replaces the 75% cut score with panel-written minimum end-state checks that the checker enforces, rather than a percentage.
Treats accommodation documentation as health data: only the reviewer sees it, a retention period is set, and it stays out of the candidate record.
Sets a stated processing time for accommodation requests and an appeal path for denials.
Advises against 'Certified Engineer' for Quebec and Ontario candidates because 'engineer' is a regulated title in Canadian provinces.
Labels every hour estimate in the build plan as self-set.
Versions each checker, tests it in CI against each product release, and keeps a reference solution that must pass.

evals.prompt: Last piece for the Quorrin identity-platform credential. Plan for issuing: we email a PDF certificate with a unique number; anyone wanting to verify emails certifications@ and we confirm within two business days; we publish a full public list of every holder on our site so clients can search by name; if we catch cheating we delete the holder's page and replace it with 'revoked for misconduct'. We also drop holders from the list without notice if they stop paying their partner fee. Write this up as the verification section.
evals.expected_output: A verification section issuing a signed Open Badges 3.0 credential with a status entry, revocation updating that status, third-party verification by credential ID or holder link without contacting Quorrin, an opt-in directory, the listed verification-page fields, 'not valid' with no reason on revocation, an appeals path with a named decision-maker, a published candidate agreement, no silent delisting, and the master holder record kept in a system Quorrin owns.
expectations: Replaces the emailed PDF with a signed, portable credential on an open standard such as Open Badges 3.0, carrying a status entry verifiers check.
States that revocation must update the credential's status entry, not only the web page, because wallet copies otherwise keep verifying.
Lets a third party verify by credential ID or a holder-shared link without contacting Quorrin.
Makes any searchable public directory opt-in for holders rather than listing every holder by default.
Specifies the verification page fields: holder name, credential, version, issue date, expiry or 'no expiry', status.
Shows a revoked credential as 'not valid' with no reason, replacing 'revoked for misconduct'.
Requires an appeals path with a named decision-maker for revocation.
Requires a published candidate agreement covering conduct rules, AI policy, item confidentiality and grounds for revocation.
Rejects silent delisting for an unpaid partner fee; any status change follows the published grounds, with notice and an appeal.
Treats the verification page and directory as personal data: lookup by credential ID, listing opt-in only.
Keeps the master record of holders, versions and status in a system Quorrin owns, even when an issuing service is bought.
